cincinnati.intro: All eight trees here stand inside one gate. Spring Grove Cemetery and Arboretum, founded in 1845, keeps a run of Ohio state champions, each marked by a small boulder and sign, and one of them is the largest September elm known in the country. A yellow buckeye older than the cemetery survives from the Mill Creek floodplain. A dawn redwood from the 1948 seed stands beside a cedar of Lebanon raised from 1930 cuttings, and a hardy rubber tree and a katsura share one stop in Section 53.
cincinnati.meta_description: Eight champion trees in Cincinnati's Spring Grove Cemetery: a yellow buckeye older than the cemetery and the largest known September elm in the US.
cincinnati.question_meta: Cincinnati's oldest tree on this map is a yellow buckeye at Spring Grove Cemetery, older than the cemetery's founding in 1845.
cincinnati.question_answer: The oldest tree on our Cincinnati map is the yellow buckeye in Section 22 of Spring Grove Cemetery and Arboretum, at 4521 Spring Grove Ave. The cemetery was founded in 1845 and says this tree was already standing.
cincinnati.question_context: Nobody has published a closer date, so older than the cemetery is the whole of what can be said, and it is a good deal. Spring Grove describes the buckeye as a survivor of the Mill Creek floodplain community of yellow buckeye, American elm and sycamore that grew here before the grounds were laid out. It is also the Ohio state champion of its species, 452 centimetres round and 31.7 metres tall on the state register. Most of the other champions at Spring Grove have younger, better documented origins. The dawn redwood in Section 18 came from the seed distributed in 1948, after the species was found alive in China. The cedar of Lebanon beside it descends from 19 cuttings sent by the Arnold Arboretum in 1930, after the cemetery's first cedar died of the cold. The bald cypress near the Fleischmann Mausoleum, 120 metres from the buckeye, has the largest girth of the eight at 538 centimetres, and its age has never been published. Each champion carries a small boulder with a State Champion sign, and the map is available from the Customer Service Center.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cincinnati?
faq.a: On this map it is the yellow buckeye in Section 22 of Spring Grove Cemetery. The cemetery was founded in 1845 and says the tree predates it. No closer date has been published.

faq.q: How do you find the champion trees at Spring Grove?
faq.a: Each one is marked by a small boulder with a State Champion sign. The Customer Service Center has a free self-guided map, and cars may drive the grounds.

faq.q: Is it free to visit Spring Grove's trees?
faq.a: Visitor listings say entry and parking are free, and the grounds open daily from 8am to 6pm, until 8pm on Monday and Thursday from May through August. It is an active cemetery, so stay on the roads and paths.

faq.q: Why is a dawn redwood at Spring Grove so special?
faq.a: The species was known only from fossils until living trees were found in China in the 1940s. Spring Grove's Ohio champion comes from the first seed distributed in 1948, and it is already 505 centimetres round.

st-louis.intro: Coal smoke, Dutch elm disease and lightning all feature in the stories of these six trees. A bald cypress at the Missouri Botanical Garden came through the smoke that killed the Garden's evergreens. A rock elm in Tower Grove Park is injected every three years to stay alive. A basswood has its own lightning conductor. At Bellefontaine Cemetery an American elm about 200 years old helped an aerospace magnate choose his grave. And in Tower Grove stands a ring of osage oranges planted so carriages could turn around.
st-louis.meta_description: Six remarkable trees in St. Louis: a former champion elm at Bellefontaine, a coal-smoke survivor and a ring of osage oranges planted for carriages.
st-louis.question_meta: The oldest tree on our St. Louis map is the American elm at Bellefontaine Cemetery, estimated at about 200 years. Where it stands, and five more.
st-louis.question_answer: The oldest tree on our St. Louis map is the American elm in Block 308 of Bellefontaine Cemetery, on Walnut, at about 200 years by St. Louis Magazine's estimate. Another account calls it older than the cemetery, founded in 1849.
st-louis.question_context: Both figures are estimates, nobody has counted its rings, and the most recent report of it standing that we can find was updated in February 2025. If you have been since, tell us. The elm was Missouri's state champion until May 2017, when a tree in the Kansas City area beat its 342 points. James S. McDonnell, the aerospace magnate, chose his burial plot partly for it. The rival for the title of oldest depends on what you count. The Missouri Botanical Garden names a bald cypress south of Shoenberg Fountain as its oldest tree, thought to be planted around 1874, while admitting that missing records mean nobody can be sure. In Tower Grove Park a group of osage oranges near the Music Stand has been called the park's oldest, with dates running from more than 150 years to the early 1900s. The park's ring of osage oranges, which is a separate planting, went in during the late nineteenth century as a turnaround for horse-drawn carriages. Bellefontaine is free and its gates lock at five in the afternoon.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in St. Louis?
faq.a: On this map, the American elm at Bellefontaine Cemetery, at about 200 years by one estimate and older than the cemetery's 1849 founding by another. Neither is a ring count.

faq.q: Is the Bellefontaine elm still the Missouri champion?
faq.a: No. It lost the title in May 2017 to an elm in the Kansas City area, after holding the record at 342 points.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see these trees?
faq.a: Two of the six, the white basswood and the bald cypress, are inside the Missouri Botanical Garden, which charges $16 general admission and $6 for St. Louis residents. Tower Grove Park and Bellefontaine Cemetery are free.

faq.q: Why does Tower Grove Park have a circle of osage oranges?
faq.a: The park's own map says the ring was planted in the late nineteenth century as a turnaround for horse-drawn carriages. It is now a stop on the park's Tree Walk.

indianapolis.intro: Three of these four trees are still standing because somebody here said no. Mae Kile would not sell her Irvington house to anyone who refused to promise to keep the bur oak. On the Near Eastside the sidewalk bends around the Temple Oak, and a neighbour's sharp eye in 2012 turned a doomed backyard into a park for the Nowland Oak, 350 metres away. The fourth tree needed no defending. A sycamore on the Statehouse lawn went round the Moon as a seed on Apollo 14.
indianapolis.meta_description: Four remarkable trees in Indianapolis: the Kile Oak, the Temple Oak with a sidewalk bent around it, and a sycamore that orbited the Moon as a seed.
indianapolis.question_meta: No Indianapolis tree has a settled claim to oldest. The Kile Oak and the Temple Oak are among the oldest, both estimated at several hundred years.
indianapolis.question_answer: No tree in Indianapolis has a settled claim to be the oldest. The Kile Oak, a bur oak on East Beechwood Avenue in Irvington, and the Temple Oak, a chinkapin oak at Temple Avenue and Brookside Parkway South Drive, are among the oldest, both estimated at several hundred years.
indianapolis.question_context: Neither tree has been cored or ring-counted, and each has been called the city's oldest by somebody. The Irvington Historical Society puts the Kile Oak at 300 to 400 years, and other accounts widen that to 300 to 500. It is 483 centimetres round. The Temple Oak is the larger tree at 617 centimetres, measured by the Springdale Neighborhood Association in late 2023, with age estimates between 270 and 450 years, and the neighbourhood itself says about 400. The bands overlap almost completely, so anyone who names a winner is guessing. The third old tree, the Nowland Oak in Chinquapin Oak Park, has been given anything from about 200 to over 300 years, and it stood unnoticed behind a house until 2012. It is a short walk along Brookside Parkway from the Temple Oak, which stands on a private corner lot and is seen from the public sidewalk. The city's youngest entry has the longest journey behind it, a sycamore planted on the Statehouse lawn in 1976 from a seed that flew on Apollo 14.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Indianapolis?
faq.a: Nobody can say for certain. The Kile Oak in Irvington and the Temple Oak on the Near Eastside are among the oldest, with estimates that overlap between about 300 and 450 years. Neither has been ring-counted.

faq.q: Can you visit the Temple Oak?
faq.a: You can see it from the public sidewalk at Temple Avenue and Brookside Parkway South Drive. The tree stands on a private lot with a house, and its canopy reaches over the parkway.

faq.q: Where is the Moon Tree in Indianapolis?
faq.a: On the east lawn of the Indiana Statehouse, about 100 feet south of the Oliver P. Morton statue and 50 feet back from North Capitol Avenue. The tree itself is unmarked, and the plaque has been moved to the south side of the building.

faq.q: Can you walk between the Temple Oak and the Nowland Oak?
faq.a: Yes. They stand about 350 metres apart along Brookside Parkway South Drive, and tile markers in the sidewalk link Chinquapin Oak Park to the Temple Oak and Spades Park.

lexington-kentucky.intro: Lexington's two trees are both hard to date and easy to find. The Kentucky state champion American basswood stands behind Henry Clay's monument in Lexington Cemetery, 742 centimetres round, with a 1987 plaque saying it was alive when the Constitution was signed. Three kilometres away at McConnell Springs, a bur oak too hollow for anyone to count its rings holds its long limbs out across the trail on tall poles. The bur oak is the city's official tree, and this one has been on the same ground since before the park, or the farm before it.
lexington-kentucky.meta_description: Two old trees in Lexington, Kentucky: the state champion basswood behind Henry Clay's monument and a hollow bur oak propped on poles at McConnell Springs.
lexington-kentucky.question_meta: The oldest tree on our Lexington map is the McConnell Springs bur oak, estimated at 250 to 300 years. Its trunk is too hollow for a ring count.
lexington-kentucky.question_answer: The oldest tree on our Lexington map is the bur oak in McConnell Springs Park, at 416 Rebmann Lane, estimated at 250 to 300 years. The park says 300 and the marker beside it says more than 250.
lexington-kentucky.question_context: Neither figure can be checked. A 2022 poem on a Lexington poetry site quotes the park forester saying the trunk is mostly hollow, which leaves too few rings to read. The marker, put up by the Society of Colonial Wars with Lexington Parks and Recreation, says the oak stood witness from William McConnell's claim in the 1700s, through the Westbrook Stock Farm of the late 1800s, to the park's creation in the 1990s. Its limbs reach across the trail and rest on tall poles. A geocaching description records a second old bur oak that fell in the ice storm of February 2003. The other tree on this map, the state champion American basswood in Lexington Cemetery, has a smaller claim on age and a larger one on size. A 1987 plaque at its base says it was alive at the signing of the Constitution in 1787, which is the plaque's statement and has not been tested by anyone. Kentucky's champion listing gives it 742 centimetres round. It stands just behind the monument at Henry Clay's grave, and the cemetery opens daily from 8am to 5pm.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Lexington, Kentucky?
faq.a: On this map it is the bur oak at McConnell Springs Park, estimated at 250 to 300 years. Its trunk is too hollow for a ring count, so the figure stays an estimate.

faq.q: Where is the big basswood in Lexington Cemetery?
faq.a: Just behind the monument at Henry Clay's grave, at 833 West Main Street. A plaque stands at its base, and the trunk is 742 centimetres round on Kentucky's champion listing.

faq.q: How far is the walk to the McConnell Springs bur oak?
faq.a: Roughly 1,500 feet from the park entrance. The trails are open daily from dawn to dusk.

huntsville-alabama.intro: Both of Huntsville's trees are state champions and both are a walk away from the road, in the 538 acres of Hays Nature Preserve on the Flint River. A shellbark hickory, by the city's account the largest known in Alabama, stands 455 centimetres round on drier ground. Within a few hundred yards a water tupelo grows in an old oxbow slough, with a moss skirt on its trunk marking the usual height of the winter water. The city's trail signs lead to both, and the paths can go under after rain.
huntsville-alabama.meta_description: Two state champion trees in Huntsville's Hays Nature Preserve: Alabama's largest known shellbark hickory and a water tupelo standing in an old oxbow.
huntsville-alabama.question_meta: No age has been published for Huntsville's two mapped trees, a champion shellbark hickory and a champion water tupelo at Hays Nature Preserve.
huntsville-alabama.question_answer: Nobody has published the age of either tree on our Huntsville map. Both stand in Hays Nature Preserve, at 7153 US-431 South, and both are state champions, a shellbark hickory 455 centimetres round and a water tupelo in the old Flint River oxbow.
huntsville-alabama.question_context: Size is what can be said with some confidence, and even there the sources are thin. The City of Huntsville, which owns the preserve through its Green Team, gives the hickory as 179 inches around and 96 feet tall, with a crown averaging 74 feet, and calls it the largest known in Alabama. For the tupelo the city's trail signs give no figures at all and speak of champion trees in the plural. A retired forester who walked the slough on 3 November 2022 estimated the base of a champion at a good nine feet across at the ground, and described a moss skirt on the trunk at about navel height, marking the usual winter water line. He placed the two champions within a few hundred yards of each other, reached from the Flint River picnic area. The hickory's sign comes after the Beaver Dam on the city's list. The pins on these pages mark the preserve as a whole, so the signs are the better guide. The preserve is free, and the dirt trails can be muddy or under water.

faq.q: How old are the champion trees at Hays Nature Preserve?
faq.a: No age has been published for either the shellbark hickory or the water tupelo. If you know more, tell us.

faq.q: How do you find the champion hickory?
faq.a: Follow the city's trail signs, where the champion hickory comes after the Beaver Dam. It stands on drier ground just off the old oxbow slough, within a few hundred yards of the champion tupelo.

faq.q: Can you reach the water tupelo all year?
faq.a: The slough floods seasonally, and the trail can be muddy or partly under water. A dry spell is the better time to go.

birmingham-alabama.intro: Birmingham's tree on this map is a small one with a good reason to be here. Alabama's champion green hawthorn started along a fence row in Ware, a mining community on ground that is now Red Mountain Park, and nobody knows whether a person or a bird put it there. The Alabama Forestry Commission named it state champion in November 2025, after a volunteer from Jefferson County Greenways researched its past. It stands beside the South BMRR Trail, across from the Pollinator Garden at the far west end.
birmingham-alabama.meta_description: Alabama's champion green hawthorn, about 125 years old, grew from a fence row in the Ware mining community and now stands in Red Mountain Park.
birmingham-alabama.question_meta: The tree on our Birmingham map is a champion green hawthorn in Red Mountain Park, about 100 to 130 years old, from a mining community's fence row.
birmingham-alabama.question_answer: The tree we have mapped in Birmingham is the champion green hawthorn in Red Mountain Park, beside the South BMRR Trail across from the Pollinator Garden, at about 100 to 130 years old. It is the only one we have dated here, so it answers for itself rather than for the city.
birmingham-alabama.question_context: The two accounts of its beginning differ a little. Jefferson County Greenways says it sprouted along a fence row in the mining community of Ware around 1900, and that nobody knows whether it was planted or sown by a bird. Bham Now says it was planted in the late 1800s and gives about 125 years. Either way it dates from the years when this ground was a place where miners lived, and it was still there when the land became Red Mountain Park. The Alabama Forestry Commission named it state champion in November 2025, after a Greenways volunteer researched its history and put it forward, and Greenways calls it a living monument to a past time. A hawthorn is a small tree, thorny and many-branched, which is how you can tell it from the oaks and pines along the trail. No girth or height has been published that we can stand behind. The park charges nothing for entry or parking and opens daily from 7am; sources disagree on the closing hour, so check before you go.

faq.q: Where is the champion hawthorn in Red Mountain Park?
faq.a: Beside the South BMRR Trail, across from the Pollinator Garden at the far west end of the trail. The park entrances are on Frankfurt Drive and Venice Road.

faq.q: How old is the Red Mountain Park hawthorn?
faq.a: Roughly 100 to 130 years. One account says it sprouted around 1900, and another says it was planted in the late 1800s.

faq.q: Is Red Mountain Park free?
faq.a: Yes, with no admission or parking fee, though donations are welcome. It opens daily at 7am, and sources disagree on whether it closes at 5pm or 7pm.
